# Methodology {#sec-methodology}

This study evaluates coding-agent harnesses as part of a complete model--harness system. The central experimental principle is to preserve behavior that belongs to the harness while controlling external differences that would otherwise distort the comparison. Native capabilities such as delegation and provider-specific compaction therefore remain enabled where supported, whereas routing, context limits, model selection, and usage accounting are constrained when necessary to keep measurements comparable.

## Benchmark and task selection

DeepSWE v1.1 was selected during planning in July--August 2026 because it was a current public benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish frontier coding agents on original, long-horizon software-engineering tasks. Its grading also fits this study: submissions are evaluated by isolated functional verifiers with a binary pass/fail reward rather than by an LLM judge [@huang2026deepswe]. This provides a reproducible success criterion without constructing and validating a new internal task set.

Running the complete benchmark across all model--harness combinations was outside the available budget. A deterministic subset of ten tasks was therefore selected from the public DeepSWE v1.1 results. For each programming language, one hard and one medium task was selected. Difficulty is derived from the solve rate of valid historical `mini-swe-agent` runs. The reference panel excludes Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Luna, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Kimi K3 because these were the four model configurations considered benchmark targets when the task sample was selected on 2026-08-18. Their own public DeepSWE results were therefore not allowed to influence the task difficulty or token-intensity values used for sampling. The final model matrix changed later; this exclusion set is part of the historical sampling procedure rather than a description of the final evaluated models. Hard tasks occupy the 75th--100th difficulty percentile, including exactly 75, while medium tasks occupy the 50th percentile up to but excluding 75. Within each language and difficulty stratum, the task with the highest median historical token usage is selected. This deliberately favors demanding tasks on which differences in context handling and token efficiency are more likely to become visible.

The selection was run on 2026-08-18 using the then-current public DeepSWE v1.1 API responses. `data/deepswe_task_selection_v1.1.json` records the resulting task IDs together with SHA-256 hashes of the `tasks.json`, `trials.json`, and `release.json` responses used at that time. The committed task IDs define the fixed task set for the experiment; the hashes provide provenance for the historical sampling inputs. Reproducing the benchmark therefore uses the committed task set rather than rerunning the selection against later API data. The complete selection procedure is implemented in `scripts/select_deepswe_tasks.py`.

## Model and harness selection

The harness set consists of Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, Pi, and OpenCode V2. Claude Code and Codex represent first-party coding agents from major model providers. OpenCode was the second-most common first-choice harness in the internal survey described in @sec-current-state, while Pi provides a comparatively lightweight alternative. OpenCode V2 was selected instead of V1 because it is the current major redesign and is more representative of the tool's future development.

The model set spans several providers and price classes: Claude Opus 5 at medium reasoning, and GPT-5.6 Luna, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash at max reasoning. The purpose is not to identify the strongest model in isolation, but to determine whether harness behavior remains effective across different model families.

## Experimental controls

Each trial evaluates exactly one model through one harness. Harness-native delegation remains enabled because subagent orchestration is part of the behavior under study. However, delegated calls are constrained to the same benchmark model as the parent session. This prevents a nominally single-model trial from becoming a multi-model ensemble. The Pier adapters aggregate usage across the complete parent/child session tree while retaining the root session as the main trajectory.

Provider-specific harness optimizations are otherwise retained. For example, a harness may use its native compaction or caching behavior when the selected model supports it. Equivalent features are not recreated through custom plugins in competing harnesses, because the objective is to evaluate the harnesses as practical systems rather than force their internal implementations to be identical.

GPT-5.6 Luna supports a larger API context window, but the first-party Codex 0.151.0 model profile uses 272,000 tokens as its default context window and requires an explicit override to use more [@codex0151ModelCatalog]. OpenAI also applies higher pricing when a request exceeds 272,000 input tokens [@openaiGpt56Luna]. The experiment therefore adopts the same 272,000-token operating window recommended by the first-party Codex default for every harness. Allowing only some harnesses to use the larger window would make cost depend on inconsistent context configuration and could move one harness into a different pricing tier.

External web-search capability is disabled in the benchmark configuration wherever the harness exposes a controllable search tool. This keeps trials limited to the repository, benchmark environment, and harness-native development tools rather than allowing external information retrieval.

### Model profiles

Where a harness ships a provider or model profile for a tested model, that profile is used as the base configuration. Only settings required to reach the designated inference endpoint are changed, such as the base URL, credentials, or gateway-facing model identifier. Harness-supplied compatibility settings, reasoning mappings, context and output limits, and other model-specific behavior are retained unless they conflict with an experimental control defined in this chapter. A custom profile is introduced only when the pinned harness version has no usable entry for the tested model or when the selected provider route requires narrowly scoped transport metadata.

Pi follows this policy for the tested open-weight models. For example, the Kimi K3 configuration retains Pi 0.84.4's bundled Moonshot/Kimi compatibility metadata while overriding the provider endpoint and API key. The GLM configuration follows the same principle. OpenCode V2 is configured analogously: built-in catalogue entries are reused where available, while explicit model metadata is supplied only for models absent from the pinned catalogue or for required transport compatibility.

Codex 0.151.0 ships a native profile for GPT-5.6 Luna, so Luna uses that profile with only the endpoint and authentication path redirected [@codex0151ModelCatalog]. The same Codex release does not ship native profiles for Claude Opus 5, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, or GLM-5.3-Flash. Unknown models instead receive a minimal fallback descriptor without configured multi-agent mode or tool mode, model-specific reasoning levels, and several other profile features available to recognized models [@codex0151FallbackMetadata]. Using this fallback would therefore evaluate those models with a substantially reduced Codex capability set.

For Claude Opus 5, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash, the experiment derives Codex metadata from the frozen GPT-5.6 Sol profile in Codex 0.151.0 and replaces the model-specific identity, context, modality, reasoning, and compatibility fields required for each route. These entries use Multi-Agent V1 and disable Responses Lite for the non-OpenAI routes while retaining the remaining Sol-derived behavior. This is a documented profile intervention rather than a neutral configuration choice: it is used so that these models are evaluated with the broader Codex agent feature set available to recognized models instead of the intentionally minimal unknown-model fallback. Codex results for these models are therefore conditional on this profile configuration.

### Model routing

All non-Anthropic model traffic is routed through AiOrbit, the internal LiteLLM proxy used by the organization. The open-weight models are served through Fireworks behind this proxy. Anthropic models are the exception and call the Anthropic API directly. This routing path is kept constant for a given model across harnesses.

AiOrbit and Fireworks are infrastructure outside the experimental manipulation. Either may transform requests or introduce provider-side failures that the study cannot control. The results therefore characterize the harnesses under this fixed deployment path rather than an abstract provider-independent environment.

## Benchmark infrastructure

The experiment does not use upstream Pier unchanged. It uses the project-specific `FZR-forks/pier` fork, which has diverged materially from the upstream runner used by DeepSWE [@pierUpstream; @pierFzrFork]. The fork became necessary because the selected model--harness matrix required additional adapters, stricter model isolation, and more complete usage accounting than upstream Pier exposed at the time of the experiment.

The fork adds Pi and OpenCode V2 support, complete delegated-session accounting for Claude Code and Codex, hard same-model enforcement for delegated calls, corrections for Codex cumulative token snapshots and inherited child history, cache-write-aware token and cost accounting, support for the internal CA required to reach AiOrbit, and preservation of failed retry-attempt evidence. Some Claude Code trajectory changes were selectively backported from Harbor; other changes are specific to this experiment. As a result, the PA1 runner is substantially more capable for this benchmark matrix than the upstream Pier checkout and must be treated as a distinct, versioned part of the experimental apparatus rather than as stock Pier.

These changes were kept outside the benchmark task itself. They affect agent installation, routing, model enforcement, trajectory conversion, and measurement, but do not modify the DeepSWE task description, repository, verifier, or reward calculation presented to the agent.

### OpenCode V2 integration

OpenCode V2 was selected instead of V1 after the V2 branch had become the actively developed redesign, but it was initially deferred because its interface and provider behavior were still changing during benchmark preparation. It was admitted only after a dedicated adapter and acceptance suite could be validated against the packaged binary. The experiment freezes OpenCode V2 at version 2.0.8. The version, platform-specific archive checksums, model catalogue, and provider configuration are pinned in the PA1 benchmark configuration rather than hardcoded into Pier, keeping the adapter generic across V2 releases.

OpenCode V2 uses a separate Pier adapter instead of reusing the V1 integration because V2 exposes a server- and session-oriented interface. Each trial starts its own private authenticated OpenCode server; servers are not shared between trials. After execution, the adapter waits for the session tree to settle and collects paginated root, delegated, utility, and compaction-session records. These records are converted into recursive usage totals while avoiding replay double-counting. Incomplete collection, provider failures, cancellations, and server termination remain visible in the trajectory; complete token and cost aggregates are withheld when the collected session tree cannot be established as complete.

Native delegation remains enabled, but model isolation required an additional control. OpenCode 2.0.8 allows the subagent tool to select any model exposed by the catalogue, so pinning only the root agent is insufficient. Restricted benchmark trials therefore disable catalogue fetching, load a frozen catalogue narrowed to the selected model and reasoning variant, and enforce that selection across root, delegated, utility, and compaction requests. This preserves OpenCode's native multi-agent behavior while preventing a nominal single-model trial from silently becoming a multi-model system.

Provider metadata and transport are kept separate where possible. Luna retains OpenCode's built-in OpenAI Responses profile so that provider-specific behavior such as native compaction is preserved. Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash retain their canonical OpenCode model identities while the transport package, gateway endpoint, and provider-facing model identifier are redirected to the fixed Fireworks-backed route. GLM additionally marks Fireworks as the transport-level canonical provider because OpenCode's Z.AI transform otherwise adds provider-specific request fields that the Fireworks route rejects. These changes are limited to transport compatibility rather than replacing the model with a synthetic provider profile.

Two further controls were required for comparability. First, OpenCode did not reliably project its configured output limit into OpenAI-compatible requests, so each affected model explicitly injects its output ceiling into the request body [@opencodeIssue47398]. Second, the same context and reasoning controls used by the other harnesses are applied: primary open-weight and Luna runs use the configured `max` reasoning variant, Opus uses `medium`, and Luna is held to the common 272,000-token operating window. No custom retry algorithm was added to OpenCode; its native retry behavior remains part of the harness, while Pier's whole-trial retry remains restricted to transport or gateway failures.

Before a primary OpenCode run is admitted, the configuration is checked with the pinned real binary rather than only by static model resolution. The acceptance path covers both the Chat Completions and Responses transports, explicit output caps, model restriction, usage reconciliation, native compaction, simultaneous-trial isolation, and a dedicated delegation smoke test. The smoke runs use low reasoning and small output limits only to validate the integration and do not change the primary benchmark settings.

## Compatibility interventions

Compatibility changes are permitted only when they are required to make a harness communicate correctly with the intended model endpoint. Such changes are kept narrowly scoped and are not used to add capabilities to a harness.

### Codex with third-party models

Codex 0.151.0 uses the OpenAI Responses protocol, while the Fireworks-backed models are reached through AiOrbit using Chat Completions. Direct translation through the LiteLLM gateway was not sufficient for Codex's request and reasoning semantics. A pinned CLIProxyAPI instance is therefore used as a protocol bridge:

`Codex -> Responses -> CLIProxyAPI -> Chat Completions -> AiOrbit -> Fireworks`.

The bridge performs protocol translation only. Its own retries, credential cooldowns, and model fallbacks are disabled so it cannot improve the measured harness behavior.

During the benchmark period, an upstream CLIProxyAPI defect was identified in which a streamed chunk containing both `reasoning_content` and visible `content` could produce an invalid Responses item order [@cliproxyIssue5659]. Rather than upgrade the complete bridge and introduce unrelated changes, the benchmark keeps the frozen v7.2.146 base and backports only the upstream fix [@cliproxyFix5659]. Logs from the completed 2026-08-31 Kimi K3 trial runs showed that the defect's triggering condition did not occur, so those runs were retained.

## Cost accounting

Cross-harness cost is calculated from recorded token and cache usage using a frozen pricing table in `benchmark/pricing.yaml`. Official model API prices are used rather than the invoice price of the underlying proxy or inference host. This separates model and harness efficiency from provider-specific discounts or surcharges.

If a trial is discarded and repeated because of a transport or gateway failure, tokens consumed by the discarded attempt remain part of the reported cost. Removing them would systematically favor configurations that fail more often. In contrast, benchmark task timeouts are treated as outcomes of the evaluated system rather than infrastructure failures and are not automatically rerun.

## Reproducibility

The selected DeepSWE task IDs are fixed in `data/deepswe_task_selection_v1.1.json`, while the runnable benchmark software is pinned separately. The standard benchmark wave uses DeepSWE revision `0b9fabbb63b9104d678fe965e1632f2dd9eaa2ea`, Pier revision `b0acdae033425500e968ac917acffeafd35f9cdb`, Codex CLI 0.151.0, Claude Code 2.1.251, Pi 0.84.4, and OpenCode V2 2.0.8. OpenCode additionally pins the platform-specific package checksums and the frozen 2.0.8 model catalogue. The compatibility-bridge image digest, model profiles, pricing table, generated configurations, and task-selection audit data are stored with the benchmark setup. Pier writes a `lock.json` into each result directory so that every run can be traced to the exact configuration used. All model runs in this standard wave use the same frozen runner and harness setup.

## Historical 2026-08-31 Kimi K3 batch

The Kimi K3 Pi, Claude Code, and Codex runs completed on 2026-08-31 are the only retained exception to the standard configuration above. They were completed before the final web-search policy and before the OpenCode V2 adapter was added, so they are documented separately rather than making their older setup appear to be the baseline for the rest of the experiment.

The first difference is the web-search tool surface. Web search had not yet been explicitly disabled in the 2026-08-31 Kimi configurations. Later testing showed that search could be available through some harness/provider combinations, which motivated explicitly disabling it for subsequent benchmark configurations. The retained Kimi logs were checked and contain no evidence of a completed Internet-backed search, so there is no observed indication that external information affected those results. Nevertheless, the tool-surface difference is kept visible as a methodological limitation. The later OpenCode V2 Kimi run retains web search as well so that the four Kimi harness results remain comparable to the already completed 2026-08-31 batch rather than changing the available tool set for only one harness.

The second difference is the Pier revision. The 2026-08-31 runs used `ff65bae55c9a8ff15ddd3c2967c81a936713dd4d`, while the standard wave uses `b0acdae033425500e968ac917acffeafd35f9cdb`. Comparing these revisions shows that the functional addition is the new OpenCode V2 adapter and its supporting registration, tests, and configuration hooks. The existing Pi, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode V1 adapters are unchanged; the only shared installed-agent change adds a hook for redacting process-environment metadata in debug logs without changing the environment passed to the process. Because the historical Kimi runs use Pi, Claude Code, and Codex rather than OpenCode V2, these Pier changes are not expected to alter their task execution, model behavior, or accounting. The older Kimi measurements are therefore retained rather than rerun solely to align the runner commit.
